newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE says Bosnia vote fair, shuns Moslem protest.
newsitem.headline: OSCE says Bosnia vote fair, shuns Moslem protest.

text.p: International supervisors of Bosnia's first postwar elections said on Sunday independent monitors had found them largely free and fair, all but dismissing a Moslem refusal to accept results from Serb areas.

France and Germany joined Richard Holbrooke, U.S. architect of the Dayton peace accords who witnessed Saturday's poll, in praising the elections, piling pressure on the Moslems to rescind their challenge.

Bosnian Serbs responded to the Moslems' rejection by ordering local election committees on Sunday to stop counting votes in Serb areas, where roughly 20,000 mostly Moslem refugees cast ballots, though they were to resume later on Sunday.

The refugees were allowed to return to their former homes under the watchful eye of heavily-armed NATO-led peace troops to cast their votes, crossing ethnic boundaries that were closed during the war and since.
International sponsors had prepared for post-election protests and obstruction by Bosnian factions still polarised after 43 months of war and said they were confident disputes would be ironed out.

The OSCE said all Bosnia's factions knew in advance the elections would not be immaculate and the preliminary evidence gave no cause to annul the results in any of Bosnia's divided Moslem, Croat and Serb-dominated sectors.

"They were almost entirely free of abuse. The international observers, according to our preliminary reports, have been well satisfied with the arrangements they observed," said OSCE spokeswoman Agota Kuperman.

"All major political parties including the (Moslem) SDA agreed to participate in these elections, knowing full well that a state of perfection in so far as political behaviour is concerned had not been achieved.
Preliminary results from the balloting for a three-person Bosnian presidency and parliaments were not expected until Monday.

The protest by Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic's Party of Democratic Action was addressed to the U.N. Security Council, the ultimate arbiter of Bosnia's peace process, but Holbrooke and other international officials shrugged it off.

"We always knew there would be protests about the elections. I assumed an SDA protest. But this was a general protest clearly (drafted) before the elections," Holbrooke told reporters in Sarajevo on Sunday. "It is not a big deal."
SDA spokesman Ismet Grbo insisted the protest was serious.

He said the number of registered Serb voters reported by Serb media exceeded the number of Serbs living in Bosnia during the 1991 census, basis of the elections. There were also far more polling stations than OSCE monitors, he noted.
Asked what the SDA would do if the OSCE appeals committee rejected its protest, Grbo told Reuters: "The international community is idealising the situation in describing the (conduct of) elections.
"We expect a firm answer on the number of registered Serbs from the OSCE this afternoon and then we'll take our position."

Jovan Zametica, adviser to acting Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic, said the SDA's move was predictable because Moslems, as the demographically largest nation in Bosnia, "have always tried to dominate it".
Plavsic's ultra-nationalist Serb Democratic Party presided over the conquest of part of Bosnia from which Moslems and Croats were evicted in 43 months of war.

Although Plavsic has heartened international peace coordinators by pledging Serb participation in post-election inter-ethnic government, analysts believe the pro-secession Serbs will try to paralyse the endeavour at every opportunity.
